summary: Describes protocol-specific procedures and RSVP-TE extensions for end-to-end recovery of Label Switched Paths in GMPLS networks, covering both protection and restoration. A companion document, RFC 4426, covers the generic functional description. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: If a road closes, traffic needs a backup road. This note explains how the network sets up and switches to backup routes from start to finish.

questions: how does gmpls end-to-end recovery work
what is lsp protection and restoration
what is the rsvp protection object
subtitle: How RSVP-TE signals backup paths and the switch to them when a GMPLS path fails.

tldr.problem: When a Label Switched Path in a GMPLS network fails, the end nodes need a standard way to set up backup paths and agree on switching traffic to them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends RSVP-TE with a PROTECTION object, a PRIMARY_PATH_ROUTE object and an ASSOCIATION object, and defines Notify-based switchover, preemption and reversion procedures for five recovery types.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3471. It has been updated by RFC 4873, RFC 6780 and RFC 9270.

today: RFC 4872 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 3471 and has itself been updated by RFC 4873, RFC 6780 and RFC 9270.

sections.title: End-to-End Recovery in GMPLS
sections.content:
Recovery is the RFC's word for both protection and restoration. They differ in how recovery resources are allocated. This document gives the RSVP-TE signaling for end-to-end recovery, meaning recovery of a whole LSP from its head-end (ingress) to its tail-end (egress). The generic functional description is in the companion RFC 4426.

Working LSPs are assumed to be resource-disjoint, so that a link, node or shared risk link group does not take down both a working LSP and its protecting LSP. Disjointness is necessary but not sufficient for recoverability. The document covers four families.

  • 1+1 protection, unidirectional and bidirectional
  • 1:N (N >= 1) protection with extra-traffic
  • Pre-planned rerouting without extra-traffic, including shared mesh
  • Full LSP rerouting

RSVP-TE Fast Reroute (RFC 4090) is not affected, because FRR implementations ignore the new objects. Crankback and segment recovery (RFC 4873) are covered elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: When a road breaks, a spare road should already be planned. This memo explains how the spare roads are marked on the map and how drivers agree to switch.

sections.title: LSP Status and Association
sections.content:
Every LSP in a recovery scheme carries a few status bits. The S (Secondary) bit separates primary LSPs, which are fully established with resources committed at the data plane, from secondary LSPs, which exist only in the control plane. The P (Protecting) bit separates working from protecting LSPs. A secondary working LSP is not valid. The O (Operational) bit is set when a protecting LSP is carrying the normal traffic after a switch.

The LSP Protection Type says which scheme applies: Full LSP Rerouting, Pre-planned Rerouting without Extra-traffic (called shared mesh when the resources are not pre-reserved for a single sender and receiver pair), LSP Protection with Extra-traffic, or Dedicated LSP Protection. A Notification (N) bit says whether the control plane is used only for notification, because the data plane does its own switching.

The ASSOCIATION object ties working and protecting LSPs together. On the working LSP its Association ID names the protecting LSP, and on the protecting LSP it names the protected LSP. Both LSPs share the same SESSION object and differ only in LSP ID.
sections.plainLanguage: Each path wears name tags: is it the main road or the spare, is it ready to drive on, and is it being used right now. Another tag says who its partner road is.

sections.title: 1+1 and 1:N Protection
sections.content:
In 1+1 unidirectional protection (section 5) a protecting LSP is signaled over a dedicated disjoint path and traffic is sent on both LSPs at once. The egress selects whichever is valid, so the two ends need no coordination. Both LSPs are fully instantiated, so no resources are shared and no extra-traffic can be carried. Setting the N bit is RECOMMENDED.

In 1+1 bidirectional protection (section 6) both ends must receive from the same LSP, so they coordinate. An end node that detects failure starts receiving on the protecting LSP and reliably sends a Notify message, with MESSAGE_ID and ACK_Desired set, using the new code/sub-code Notify Error/LSP Failure (Switchover Request). The other end switches too and answers with a Notify carrying a MESSAGE_ID_ACK object (the Switchover Response), and the first end then sends an Ack.

In 1:1 protection with extra-traffic (section 7) the protecting LSP is also fully provisioned but may carry preemptable extra-traffic, which is disconnected when a switch happens. The same request and response exchange is used, with the end node first disconnecting the extra-traffic. Section 7.3 extends this to 1:N (N > 1), where one protecting LSP serves N working LSPs between the same endpoints and the Protection Type is 0x04. After the switch, the protecting LSP SHOULD be signaled with the O bit set.
sections.plainLanguage: With 1+1, you send the same message down two roads at once and the receiver picks whichever arrives. With 1:1, the spare road carries only low-priority traffic that is kicked off when it is needed.

sections.title: Rerouting and Shared-Mesh Restoration
sections.content:
In rerouting without extra-traffic (section 8) the working LSP is primary and the protecting LSP is secondary: S and P are both set to 1 on the protecting LSP, its resources are pre-reserved in the control plane but not committed at the data plane, and it can carry no extra-traffic. The head-end is notified through a Notify message and activates the secondary LSP by sending a modified Path message with the S bit set to 0. Activation can also be done upstream using a Resv message, if configured locally.

Shared-mesh restoration (section 9) lets several secondary LSPs share recovery resources when the working LSPs they protect are disjoint. The Path message for a secondary LSP SHOULD include at least one PRIMARY_PATH_ROUTE object, which lists the links and nodes used by the protected LSP so that each node can check disjointness before sharing. If the protected paths overlap, the node SHOULD NOT share the link and may return a PathErr such as Admission Control Failure/LSP Admission Failure.

Full LSP rerouting (section 11) establishes the alternate route only after the failure, selected at the head-end. It uses make-before-break with the Shared-Explicit reservation style, so the new LSP, which differs only in LSP ID, does not double-count shared resources.
sections.plainLanguage: A spare road can be reserved without being built, and several drivers can reserve the same spare because their main roads are far apart. If a main road breaks, the spare is finished and opened.

sections.title: Preemption, Reversion and Recovery Commands
sections.content:
Resources pre-reserved for a secondary LSP MAY be used by lower-priority LSPs, and they MUST be preempted when the protecting LSP is activated (section 10). The preempting node de-allocates the resources, sends PathTear and PathErr messages with the new code Policy Control failure/Hard preempted, reserves the resources for the protecting LSP, and only then sends the Path message. This ordering avoids misconnection of the downstream path.

Reversion (section 12) returns normal traffic to the working LSP once it has recovered. For 1+1 bidirectional, 1:N and rerouting schemes, the A bit of ADMIN_STATUS is cleared first. The source then sends traffic on both LSPs and reliably sends a Notify with Notify Error/LSP Recovered (Switchback Request), the destination switches back and confirms, and the source acknowledges. Finally the O bit is cleared on the protecting LSP, or for rerouting without extra-traffic the protecting LSP is deactivated by setting the S bit to 1.

Section 13 maps operator recovery commands onto signaling. A new Lockout (L) bit in the ADMIN_STATUS object makes a recovery LSP temporarily unavailable. Setting the O bit locks out normal traffic. Forced and requested switches reuse the switchover procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: If a spare road must take over, any slow traffic using it is asked to leave first. When the main road is fixed, everyone agrees together to move back before the spare is released.

sections.title: The PROTECTION, PRIMARY_PATH_ROUTE and ASSOCIATION Objects
sections.content:
The PROTECTION object (Class-Num 37, C-Type 2) holds the S, P, N and O bits, 6 bits of LSP (Protection Type) Flags and 6 bits of Link Flags. A value of 0 in the LSP flags means Unprotected, and only one value SHOULD be set at a time. A node that cannot satisfy the requested type MUST send a PathErr with Routing problem/Unsupported LSP Protection.

The PRIMARY_PATH_ROUTE object (Class-Num 38, C-Type 1) is a list of subobjects (IPv4 address, IPv6 address, Label and Unnumbered Interface) copied from the route of the protected LSP. It is only for secondary protecting LSPs with Protection Type 0x02. An empty object is illegal.

The ASSOCIATION object (Class-Num 199, C-Type 1 for IPv4 and 2 for IPv6) has a 16-bit Association Type (1 means Recovery), a 16-bit Association ID and an Association Source address. Transit nodes pass it on unchanged. Section 17 shows where these objects fit in the Path and Resv messages.
sections.plainLanguage: These are three forms the routers fill in: one says what kind of backup this is, one lists the main route it covers, and one pairs the main and spare together.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The threats identified in RFC 4426 may apply to the RSVP messages used here. RSVP signaling MUST be able to provide authentication and integrity. RFC 2747 provides this for hop-by-hop exchanges. The Notify messages used by this document are not hop-by-hop, so standard IPsec-based integrity and authentication can be used as explained in RFC 3473.

Poorly applied protection raises the risk of misconnection, especially with extra-traffic, where the wrong traffic could reach the wrong destination. The RFC points to mechanisms in sections 7.2, 8.3 and 10 against this.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages saying switch the road must be genuine, or someone could send traffic to the wrong place.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC asks IANA to assign two RSVP Class Numbers (37 for PROTECTION, 38 for PRIMARY_PATH_ROUTE) plus the ASSOCIATION class number 199, and their C-Types. It defines Association Type values 0 (Reserved) and 1 (Recovery), with other values assigned by IETF Standards Track RFC action.

New error code and sub-code values are defined, such as Notify Error/LSP Failure (9), Notify Error/LSP Recovered (10) and Notify Error/LSP Locally Failed (11), all under Error Code 25. A new registry tracks ADMIN_STATUS bits, with the Lockout bit at position 26.
sections.plainLanguage: New labels need official numbers so every router reads them the same way.
